The law this sheet serves

Colour answers what kind of money. Ink is everything else. Red stays earned. Four domain hues, never five — worn identically by a record's icon well, its detail chrome, and every chart of that domain.

Why dark is authored, not inverted

Dark mode is co-primary (article 9) and §D3 explicitly forbids an inversion pass. An inverted #43823B is a mud green that loses its identity as the app accent. So the ground was chosen first, then four hues that hold identity against it.

What I did and did not invent

Not invented: the four dark domain hues. Spec §D3 already names them as light/dark pairs. Authored here: the dark ground, the dark ink ramp, three dark semantics, eight text steps, and the two light fixes §14.3 asks for.

01 · The two grounds

Warm paper, both ends. Neither ground is neutral grey — the light one is locked at #FBF9F5 and the dark one answers it in the same hue family rather than in black.

Why #14120F

Same hue family as the light paper (a warm ~35° cast), four steps of value below it rather than a hue flip. Not #000: pure black on OLED makes the hairlines vanish and the paper metaphor with it.

Elevation reverses, warmth does not

Light: card is lighter than paper. Dark: card is lighter than paper too — the step goes toward the light in both, so a card is always the raised thing. Sheets take one step further.

A third surface, new

sheet is added to the token set because §D1's task sheets and fitted pickers sit over a card-bearing parent. In light it equals card; in dark it must not.

Nothing glows

No shadow tokens change between themes: dark elevation is carried by the surface step and the hairline, never by a glow. A calm surface does not emit light.

03 · The four domain hues

Four, never five. Both halves of every pair come from spec §D3 verbatim — this sheet adds only the text step each one needs to carry type.

The rule the text steps encode: a domain hue at its base step is a graphical object — a bar, a gauge fill, detail chrome — and clears the 3:1 threshold that governs those. It is not the well colour: a well is domainWash + domainText, validated as its own pairing in §05. It carries type only at its -text step. One rule, all four, no exceptions to remember.

The one pair that needs the rule most

Dark contract #A05C96 lands at {{ r.contractDarkUi }} on a dark card — comfortably over the 3:1 graphical threshold, under the 4.5:1 text one. Since §D3 fixes that hex, the answer is not to change it but to keep it off type: a plan chip's label reads in #C489BA, its well and its bar stay #A05C96. Same for light fuel, which is {{ r.fuelLightUi }} on paper.

04 · Semantics, and the collision this sheet fixes

Reserved, never a fifth series. Two of the three needed authoring; one needed correcting.
attention
#9C5A16  /  #E8934A DARK NEW

Over-cap, overdue, the days-over capsule, the worst-value hollow dot, an open review item. Being late is a fact, not an error — this is the colour that keeps the surface from turning red.

critical
#A32D22  /  #E86458 DARK NEW

Destructive confirmations and hard validation errors only, and only ever as text. Never a fill, never a banner, never a surface. Two places in the whole app earn it.

positive
#1F6F63 CHANGED  /  #4FA795 NEW

Reserved and nearly unused. It exists so that it is not the fuel hue — and it is deliberately a teal, not a green, so the app keeps exactly one green.

§D3 reserves semantic colours and forbids using them as "series 4". With positive === accent === domain.fuel a positive state and fuel money were literally the same pixel. Teal keeps "one green in the app" intact.

Both light hexes are locked, so I left them. The dark pair I authored is separated by value instead — attention is {{ r.attentionVsService }} lighter than service. What actually carries the pair everywhere is shape: §D4's worst mark is a hollow dot against a filled one. See sheet 06.

05 · AA validation, every pair, both themes

§H4 requires AA for every semantic pair in both themes. Ratios are computed live from the hexes on this sheet, against {{ basisLabel }}.

Two thresholds apply, and which one applies is a property of the role, not of the colour: 4.5:1 for anything that carries body-size type, 3:1 for large type and for graphical objects — bars, gauge fills, chrome. Wells are not in that class: they carry a glyph, so they are held to the full 4.5:1 as a domainText-on-domainWash pair. A row marked GRAPHIC is held to 3:1 and is forbidden from carrying type; its text step is the row beneath it.

06 · Colour-blind validation

Not "do the hues survive simulation" — which pairs can ever appear as the same kind of mark, and what carries them if hue fails.

The finding that matters most: Koi never asks hue to work alone

Light fuel and light service sit at {{ r.fuelLightUi }} and {{ r.serviceLightUi }} — near-identical luminance, and under deuteranopia both collapse toward the same yellow. That would be disqualifying in most systems. It is not here, because of two rules that were already in the spec for other reasons: §D4 gives every chart exactly one series colour, so no chart ever needs two domain hues told apart; and the one multi-hue chart in the product — Cost's Where it went — labels every bar with its name. In rows, the well carries a distinct glyph per record type and the title says what it is. Hue is always the third cue, never the first.

Two things to read here rather than take on trust. The odometer and milestone rows carry no amount — a reading is not money (inv. 16 for notes, and the trailing figure rule in §3.2). The odometer well is hairline, not a hue: distance is ink, so its well is the surface's own line weight and its glyph does the identifying. Glyphs are Lucide at 1,75 stroke, each drawn in its domain’s -text step on its domainWash well — annex B is where the eight were chosen.

08 · The token set

Shaped to replace src/ui/theme.ts's single palette with a resolved pair, which is what useKoiTheme() needs to exist.

Two code fixes that ride with this

app.json declares userInterfaceStyle: automatic while _layout.tsx pins StatusBar style="dark" — dark content on a dark ground. And #F6EFE3 in sync/provider.tsx is off-palette and should just go.

Menlo is not the data voice

Menlo is Apple-only; on Android it falls back to the proportional default and numbers start jittering — on the platform the project calls co-equal. The data voice needs a bundled tabular face, not a platform name. Sheet 02 picks it.

What this sheet does not decide

Nothing in §16. The palette touches no open owner question — the closest, #9 (income wants the positive hue §D3 reserves), stays open and is now at least costed: positive is a teal nobody else uses, so an income surface could take it without disturbing the four.
